item.title: AMD acquires AI chip startup Taalas to boost inference performance by etching model weights into silicon [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: AMD has acquired Toronto-based AI chip startup Taalas, which develops model-specific integrated circuits that etch AI model weights directly into silicon to significantly accelerate inference performance. Taalas' first test chip demonstrated serving Meta's Llama 3.1 model at nearly 17,000 tokens per second, outperforming Nvidia GPUs and Cerebras accelerators by large margins. The startup's approach involves embedding model weights in mask-ROM while using SRAM for caches and fine-tuning adapters, enabling efficient inference but limiting flexibility since any major model update requires chip respins. AMD plans to integrate Taalas' technology with its Instinct-based Helios racks, potentially offloading token generation to these specialized accelerators while handling prompt processing on GPUs, aiming to offer a high-performance AI platform for specific workloads.

item.title: OpenAI updates GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT for Plus and Pro users with more reliable facts and focused answers, expands free user access to GPT-5.6 Luna with unlimited text chats and a new Think button [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI has improved GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT for Plus and Pro users to provide more reliable factual responses and more focused, adaptable answers. The update includes a new slider to control the depth of ChatGPT's reasoning. For free users, OpenAI has expanded access to GPT-5.6 Luna, enabling unlimited text chats and introducing a Think button that allows access to higher reasoning for more complex questions. The improvements aim to support a wide range of user needs, from quick questions to complex planning and research. GPT-5.6 Sol now delivers clearer, more concise answers tailored to the question's complexity, avoiding unnecessary details and formatting. The update also enhances factual accuracy, especially for information involving dates, numbers, and rules. Free users benefit from expanded capabilities with GPT-5.6 Luna as the default model, improving accessibility to advanced AI features.

item.title: Study finds humans miss one in three AI agent command threats during 40,000 game runs simulating permission approvals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A browser game simulating human approval of AI agent commands revealed that players missed about one in three threats, with an average accuracy of 66.3% across over 40,000 runs and 409,000 approval decisions. The game tested users' ability to detect malicious commands under time pressure, highlighting challenges in human oversight of AI actions. The study found that blatantly destructive commands were caught more reliably than those exfiltrating credentials, which were missed three times as often. A notable blind spot was the command "npm run analyze," approved 64.7% of the time despite containing hidden data exfiltration scripts, indicating users often overlook detailed command histories. The findings suggest that relying on users to approve AI commands may not be a strong safeguard, especially as approval fatigue increases with repeated prompts.

item.title: New Orleans deploys AI to answer 911 calls for triage and information, routing emergencies to human dispatchers to reduce call volume [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: New Orleans' Orleans Parish Communication District has started using Carbyne's AI Emergency Call Triage system to answer 911 calls, aiming to manage high call volumes by automatically handling repeated or related calls and directing emergencies to human dispatchers. The AI was first implemented in April for 311 non-emergency calls and now assists with 911 calls by providing immediate feedback and routing callers appropriately. The AI system is designed to reduce delays caused by multiple calls about the same incident, but officials emphasize that it does not replace human dispatchers for emergency calls. While the technology may improve response efficiency, concerns remain about potential biases in AI decision-making and challenges in accurately understanding diverse speech patterns, highlighting the need for human oversight and careful monitoring.

item.title: Researchers introduce the Ignition Index to quantify Global Workspace Theory dynamics in transformer language models across multiple architectures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed the Ignition Index, a new metric that measures abrupt transitions in transformer language model layers, reflecting Global Workspace Theory's predictions. The metric distinguishes genuine linguistic processing from spurious effects and was tested across 11 models from five architecture families, showing feedforward transformers exhibit stronger ignition-like behavior than state-space models, while recurrent models show such transitions along their iteration dimension. The study also identified a phase transition during training in one model before the formation of specific attention mechanisms and found no correlation between ignition characteristics and model scale or input signal strength, suggesting a saturation effect in transformer architectures.

item.title: Researchers introduce EcoAgent-Bench to evaluate economic decision-making in budget-constrained LLM agents across 304 tasks with priced actions and explicit budgets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: EcoAgent-Bench is a new benchmark designed to assess how large language model (LLM) agents make economic decisions under budget constraints, focusing on task completion with priced actions and explicit budgets. The benchmark includes 304 tasks derived from GAIA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, testing decisions such as when to escalate, model tier selection, and stopping on unsupported premises. Seven LLM agents and four oracle controls were evaluated in tool-API and workspace-CLI settings, revealing that agents often either escalate unnecessarily or fail to escalate when needed, resulting in low economic consistency scores. The study found that micro-averaged accuracy can reward one-sided policies like always escalating, which perform poorly on save-oriented tasks, prompting the introduction of an economic-consistency score to better capture balanced performance. Tool-API agents achieved only 3.9% to 24.0% strict success rates and up to 7.3% economic consistency, with GPT-5.4's escalation rate increasing marginally from 0% to 3% under budget changes. The results highlight that task completion under budget and economical action selection are distinct challenges. The researchers have released the task bundle, transformation pipeline, evaluation environments, and result artifacts to support further study.

item.title: Research proposes a multi-layered, compliance-first AI architecture for hospitals integrating agent orchestration, policy centralization, and privacy-preserving data fabric [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Hospitals increasingly use AI for tasks like triage and scheduling, but most systems remain isolated within departments, causing duplicated efforts and governance challenges. This research introduces a hospital-specific AI platform architecture featuring an Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows, a Compliance and Policy Layer centralizing regulations such as HIPAA and GDPR, and a Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric incorporating federated learning and differential privacy. Using a synthetic hospital dataset and an open prototype, the study demonstrates coordinated triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, resulting in simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation while maintaining secure data access. The architecture offers a practical blueprint for hospital leaders to transition from fragmented AI tools to governed, globally compliant platforms adaptable to on-premise, hybrid, or cloud deployments.

item.title: Researchers introduce HarnessOpt-Bench to evaluate LLMs on automated harness optimization across multiple tasks and models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark designed to measure how well large language models (LLMs) perform automated harness optimization, which involves iteratively improving the prompts, tools, and orchestration code surrounding an AI system. The benchmark evaluates LLMs as optimizers by providing them with a seed harness, graded feedback, and a fixed evaluation budget to edit and improve the harness, with performance measured by normalized gains on held-out test data. The study tested five leading LLMs across four downstream tasks using both a shared coding harness and their native harnesses over 111 runs. Results showed that optimizer models had a greater impact than the coding harnesses they used, native harnesses were not consistently better, and performance gains varied significantly depending on the task and initial conditions. These findings establish harness optimization as a measurable capability with substantial room for improvement in AI systems.

item.title: Study finds PCA-based dimensionality reduction improves Persian speech emotion recognition using Whisper, with limited gains from ASR fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers investigated the use of Whisper, a large pretrained speech model, for Persian speech emotion recognition (SER), focusing on reducing representation dimensionality and adapting the model to the Persian language. They proposed a framework that applies principal component analysis (PCA) to frame-level embeddings from Whisper, reducing trainable parameters and improving performance on the ShEMO dataset under a speaker-independent protocol. Fine-tuning Whisper on a Persian automatic speech recognition (ASR) task provided only modest improvements for SER, indicating limited transfer from ASR adaptation to emotion recognition in this context. The PCA-based approach also reduced training latency and memory usage by eliminating the need for learned projection layers, while an attention-based pooling mechanism aggregated the reduced embeddings for classification with a lightweight prediction head. These findings offer practical insights for efficiently applying large pretrained speech models to emotion recognition tasks in low-resource languages like Persian.

item.title: Researchers propose GROM, a gradient-free one-shot machine unlearning method that rapidly removes targeted knowledge from large language models with a closed-form solution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce GROM, a novel machine unlearning technique that eliminates specific sensitive knowledge from large language models without iterative fine-tuning. Unlike traditional gradient-based methods, GROM uses a ridge-regularized least-squares optimization to compute a closed-form additive update for targeted weight matrices, applying the change in seconds through gradient-free forward passes. GROM preserves model behavior on retained data while suppressing unwanted content, achieving state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on benchmarks such as TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News, and WMDP. The method also resists low-bit quantization attacks that can recover erased content in gradient-based approaches. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further use and evaluation.

item.title: Researchers introduce AV-AIVAT for 74x cheaper agent evaluation with certified anytime-valid stopping in imperfect-information games [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present AV-AIVAT, a method combining the Action-Informed Value Assessment Tool (AIVAT) with continuously monitored Confidence Sequences (CSs) to enable efficient, auditable early stopping in agent evaluations for imperfect-information games. This approach reduces variance and allows evaluations to stop as soon as sufficient evidence is gathered, maintaining statistical guarantees. AV-AIVAT was tested across 15 large language model agent configurations in Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, showing a median 74-fold reduction in the number of hands needed to reach a decision compared to raw outcomes under asymptotic confidence sequences. The method also includes exact finite-sample certification using Empirical-Bernstein CS, demonstrated structurally for Leduc hold'em, and provides tools for third-party verification of evaluation results at stopping time.

item.title: Researchers introduce SCOPE to improve language model selective trust by reducing errors from misleading context while preserving accuracy on valid context [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers address the challenge of language models being misled by external signals that can flip correct answers to wrong ones. They introduce MIST, a human-annotated benchmark with four context conditions, and SC2W, a metric measuring susceptibility to misleading signals. Their study finds this vulnerability is widespread across models. To mitigate this, they propose SCOPE, which optimizes model training using balanced preference pairs across all context types rather than focusing only on misleading cases. This approach significantly reduces errors caused by misleading context in popular open-source models while maintaining accuracy when context is clean, correct, or irrelevant. The work emphasizes evaluating models based on selective trust rather than mere resistance to misleading information.

item.title: Researchers find test-time scaling in reasoning models often fails to improve accuracy and increases hallucinations on knowledge-intensive tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study evaluating 14 reasoning models shows that increasing inference-time computation through longer reasoning chains does not consistently enhance accuracy in closed-book knowledge-intensive tasks and often leads to more factuality hallucinations. The research identifies that longer reasoning encourages more attempts to answer, many incorrect, and reveals confirmation bias where extended reasoning reinforces early errors with fabricated details. The authors also provide an information-theoretic explanation that compute-only test-time scaling cannot introduce new information about the correct answer, highlighting limitations of current methods for these tasks.

item.title: CRINN uses reinforcement learning to optimize approximate nearest neighbor search algorithms, achieving top performance on multiple benchmark datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: CRINN introduces a new approach to approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) by framing optimization as a reinforcement learning problem that rewards execution speed while maintaining accuracy. The method automatically generates faster ANNS implementations and demonstrates superior or tied top performance on five out of six widely-used benchmark datasets compared to state-of-the-art open-source algorithms. The research highlights CRINN's potential beyond ANNS optimization by showing that large language models augmented with reinforcement learning can automate complex algorithmic improvements that typically require specialized expertise and manual effort. The code for CRINN is publicly available for further exploration and use.

item.title: Researchers propose All-Quadrant Bounded Clipping GRPO to fix unbounded updates in reinforcement learning with large language models, improving stability and generalization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers identify a structural blind spot in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) used for reinforcement learning with large language models, where negative advantage combined with increased likelihood ratio leads to unbounded suppressive updates that reduce entropy and reasoning capacity. To address this, they introduce All-Quadrant Bounded Clipping GRPO (ABC-GRPO), which applies clipping across all four quadrants of the likelihood-ratio and advantage space to ensure bounded policy updates. ABC-GRPO clips the likelihood ratio before multiplying by the advantage, adding a trust-region floor and cap in specific quadrants to maintain stable policy displacement. Evaluations on mathematical reasoning tasks with Qwen3 base models show ABC-GRPO outperforms GRPO, SAPO, and dual-clip PPO, and is competitive with the strongest baseline DAPO, while preserving higher entropy. The improvements also transfer to other benchmarks including MATH-500 and out-of-domain code generation (HumanEval). Ablation studies confirm the dominant role of the previously unbounded quadrant in limiting performance.

item.title: Researchers present Online Reasoning Calibration (ORCA) to improve large language model reasoning efficiency and generalization through test-time training and conformal prediction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Online Reasoning Calibration (ORCA), a framework that calibrates the sampling process of large language models using conformal prediction and test-time training to provide valid confidence estimates under distributional shifts. ORCA employs a meta-learning procedure that updates the calibration module for each input, addressing inefficiencies caused by miscalibration in post-trained models and sampling techniques. The method offers theoretical guarantees on conformal risks and demonstrates improved efficiency and generalization across various reasoning tasks. Empirical results show that ORCA can reduce compute costs by up to 47.5% on in-distribution tasks and significantly improve savings in zero-shot out-of-domain settings while maintaining low error rates. The code for ORCA is publicly available.

item.title: Researchers prove a fundamental trade-off in long-sequence models limiting simultaneous efficiency, compactness, and recall capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers identify and prove a fundamental trade-off in long-sequence models, showing that no model can simultaneously achieve per-step computation independent of sequence length (efficiency), state size independent of sequence length (compactness), and recall proportional to sequence length (recall). They formalize this within an Online Sequence Processor framework that includes Transformers, state space models, and recurrent networks. Using information-theoretic inequalities, they prove that models satisfying efficiency and compactness have limited recall capacity dependent on model dimension and vocabulary size. The study classifies 52 architectures published before March 2026 according to this trade-off, demonstrating that each achieves at most two of the three properties, with hybrid models tracing continuous trajectories within the trade-off space. Experiments on synthetic associative recall tasks with five representative architectures validate the theoretical bound, confirming that empirical recall capacity remains below the information-theoretic limit and no architecture escapes the trade-off triangle.

item.title: Researchers propose stage-wise preference optimization to reduce hallucination in vision-language models by targeting multimodal data near failure boundaries [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a stage-wise preference optimization framework to reduce hallucination in vision-language models (VLMs), addressing the issue where models generate linguistically plausible but visually inconsistent responses. Their approach constructs hallucination-focused preference pairs emphasizing ambiguous spatial orientation, object relationships, OCR uncertainty, and adversarial false-premise training to improve grounding consistency and reduce hallucination. Experiments on open-source benchmarks and real-world multimodal evaluations show that this method produces more visually grounded responses than several leading proprietary VLMs, particularly in challenging scenarios involving ambiguous spatial reasoning and adversarial inputs. The findings suggest hallucination arises not only from limited model capacity but also from autoregressive generation favoring plausible continuations under weak visual grounding, pointing to future research directions in physical consistency modeling and uncertainty-aware multimodal reasoning.

item.title: Researchers propose CP-MoE, a continual learning framework using a transient expert to reduce forgetting and preserve knowledge transfer in large language and vision-language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce CP-MoE, a continual learning framework designed to address catastrophic forgetting in large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) by using a transient expert to guide integration of task-specific updates into stable experts. CP-MoE employs a consistency-preserving routing bias and a transient expert-guided regularization mechanism to reduce parameter interference and forgetting while maintaining cross-task knowledge transfer. The framework was validated on unimodal and multimodal benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the SuperNI language tasks and outperforming strong baselines on the VQA v2 visual reasoning dataset.

item.title: EuroExec benchmark shows frontier language models solve only 56.9% of European executive tasks compared to near-ceiling expert performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated six leading large language models (LLMs) on EuroExec, a benchmark of 413 open-ended European executive decision tasks created by 47 domain experts. Each model response was manually assessed using a detailed rubric and preference rankings, revealing the best model solved just 56.9% of tasks while expert answers were preferred in 74% of comparisons. The study highlights that current frontier LLMs fall significantly short of professional expert standards on complex, real-world decision problems and that human evaluation remains essential for accurate assessment.

item.title: Researchers propose A-SR, a self-evolving agentic LLM framework for symbolic regression that improves formula discovery accuracy across scientific domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed A-SR, a self-evolving agentic framework for symbolic regression that coordinates formula discovery through hierarchical coordination protocols and role-conditioned evidence views. The framework adapts search processes within runs without updating LLM parameters and distills recorded trajectories into open-source LLMs across runs, improving accuracy significantly over baselines on benchmark scientific domains. A-SR routes evaluator feedback to update role-level utilities and manage elite motifs, failure traces, and diagnostics among agents. Tested on four real-world scientific discovery tasks, A-SR achieved the best normalized mean squared error on seven of eight metrics, demonstrating improved reliability and productivity in symbolic regression compared to existing LLM-guided methods.

item.title: Aleksa Gordic details vLLM, a high-throughput large language model inference system, covering its engine core, advanced features, scaling, serving layer, and benchmarks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Aleksa Gordic's blog post introduces vLLM, a modern high-throughput inference system for large language models, explaining its core components and advanced features. The post outlines the system's architecture, including the LLM engine, scheduling, paged attention, and continuous batching, and describes how it scales from single-GPU offline inference to multi-GPU, multi-node online serving. The article breaks down the engine's construction, including configuration, processing, execution, and caching mechanisms, and previews future posts that will explore subsystems in more detail. It targets readers interested in understanding state-of-the-art LLM engines and contributing to related projects.

item.title: Researchers propose Agentic Nesting framework to integrate enterprise applications as autonomous AI agents with hierarchical coordination and conversational interfaces [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: A new methodology called Agentic Nesting has been proposed to improve enterprise application integration by encapsulating existing applications as autonomous AI agents organized in a hierarchical structure. This approach aims to reduce architectural coupling and operational costs while enabling natural-language interaction and autonomous operation across heterogeneous systems. The framework includes a central orchestrator for coordinating tasks among agents and offers a unified conversational interface for cross-application querying and process management. The methodology introduces the concepts of "Application-as-Agent" and "Conversation-as-Integration," targeting enhanced intelligence capabilities and scalable coordination in complex enterprise ecosystems.

item.title: Researchers propose Woodpecker Distillation to improve strong language models by using weak models to identify and correct localized reasoning errors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Woodpecker Distillation, a training framework that enhances the reasoning performance of large language models by leveraging weak models to diagnose and correct localized reasoning bugs in stronger models. This method contrasts successful and unsuccessful weak-model interventions to create a corrective teacher distribution, which is then distilled into the strong model to guide its future reasoning steps toward correct solutions. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks demonstrate that this approach consistently improves strong-model accuracy and outperforms direct fine-tuning on corrected outputs.

item.title: Study finds guideline-based categorical encoding matches continuous predictors in stroke outcome models for two treatment cohorts, with one cohort showing accuracy drop [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A recent study evaluated whether continuous predictors in machine learning models for 90-day acute ischaemic stroke outcome prediction can be replaced by categorical encodings aligned with clinical guidelines without losing accuracy. Using data from a multi-centre European registry divided into three treatment cohorts, researchers compared standard gradient-boosted models with versions using guideline-based categorical thresholds. The categorised models performed comparably to continuous models in two cohorts but showed a significant accuracy decline in one cohort. Feature importance rankings remained consistent across models, indicating that guideline-based categorisation preserves key prognostic factors. This suggests that adopting clinical guideline-aligned categories is a feasible approach for stroke outcome prediction models.

item.title: SkillTrace introduces multi-trace provenance auditing for LLM-agent skill reuse using expression, implementation, and operational traces with Skill Operational Graphs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: SkillTrace is a framework designed to audit the reuse of skills in large language model (LLM) agent ecosystems by extracting and comparing three types of provenance traces: Expression, Implementation, and Operational. It represents the Operational Trace as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) that captures activation, procedure, and resource-flow structures, with an LLM assisting in extracting this trace during ingestion. Evaluations on the SKILLTRACE-BENCH dataset show high accuracy, and a large-scale audit demonstrates that trace-attributed evidence can improve skill reuse review beyond traditional repository-level methods.

item.title: Otter AI predicts human chess moves using time-aware, history-conditioned model with 15.3M parameters, surpassing Maia 2 on 117M Lichess rapid games [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Otter is a human chess AI that predicts moves by considering the last 20 moves and clock pressure, treating chess as a sequential, time-aware process rather than isolated positions. It was trained on 6.1 billion positions from 117 million rapid games on Lichess and achieves 55.23% top-1 move prediction accuracy, outperforming previous models like Maia 2 despite using fewer parameters and less data. The model's accuracy varies across player skill levels, peaking at 57.38% in the 1900-1999 Elo bracket. Otter's code, trained models, and training logs have been publicly released, demonstrating that incorporating move history and time control improves human move prediction in chess AI.

item.title: Researchers introduce TriQua framework for factuality evaluation balancing fact granularity and context with a new metric aligning with human judgments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed TriQua, a framework that models simple claims as standard triples and complex claims as hyperrelational facts with contextual qualifiers to improve factuality evaluation in large language models. TriQua includes TriQuaScore, a metric that quantifies factuality and shows strong alignment with human assessments. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that TriQua provides robust fact decomposition and outperforms existing methods in evidence-based fact verification.

item.title: Researchers develop benchmarks for agentic self-driving microscopy showing effectiveness for qualification but limited generalization to unseen tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers created a benchmarking and trace-logging framework to evaluate how different agent architectures impact performance in controlling microscopy tasks using large language model agents. They tested 105 agent configurations across 53 microscopy tasks with nearly 2,000 runs, comparing factors like agent number, LLM type, and retrieval-augmented generation parameters. The benchmarks effectively support qualification, regression testing, and direct comparison of agent configurations but do not reliably predict performance on new, unseen microscopy tasks, indicating limitations in generalizing agentic control systems beyond tested scenarios.

item.title: Researchers introduce DoctorAgents, an AI framework using large language model agents to iteratively refine AutoML pipelines for small clinical temporal datasets, outperforming existing methods [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed DoctorAgents, an AI framework that autonomously constructs and optimizes machine learning pipelines for small clinical temporal data by using specialized large language model agents to generate, validate, and refine models through natural language feedback. This approach replaces traditional exhaustive search with reasoning-driven refinement to better handle scarce and complex clinical data. Experiments across various clinical tasks show that DoctorAgents consistently outperforms established AutoML baselines and produces more interpretable, task-specific representations.

item.title: Researchers propose SCP-NL2TL, a selective conformal prediction framework that verifies reliability of natural language to temporal logic translations for safer autonomous system specifications [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce SCP-NL2TL, a framework that translates natural language instructions into formal temporal logic specifications while assessing their reliability to prevent unsafe or incorrect interpretations in autonomous systems. The method uses two black-box signals-back-translation fidelity and translation dispersion-to score reliability and applies conformal risk control to decide whether to accept or abstain from a specification, with an anomaly detector screening out-of-distribution inputs before translation. Experiments on Signal Temporal Logic, Linear Temporal Logic, and Spatio-Temporal Logic demonstrate improved translation accuracy, robustness to distribution shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention, establishing a foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces in safety-critical applications.

item.title: Researchers present Recursive Synthetic Terminal Tasks framework to generate 37,484 long-horizon terminal-agent tasks at $0.05 each, improving Qwen3.5 model performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Recursive Synthetic Terminal Tasks (RST), a framework that recursively synthesizes and verifies long-horizon terminal-agent tasks starting from verified seed tasks. Over fifteen rounds, RST produced 37,484 tasks with increasing complexity, maintaining stable synthesis yield and validation rates while reducing cost to approximately $0.05 per task. Task difficulty grew substantially, with reference solutions expanding from 67 to 374 lines and executed commands increasing from 40 to 244. To demonstrate training benefits, the team collected rejection-sampled Qwen3.5 trajectories on these tasks for supervised fine-tuning, resulting in up to 10-point improvements on multiple benchmarks for Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B models. Agentic PPO further boosted Qwen3.5-27B performance by 20% to 41% relative gains across benchmarks, indicating the approach's effectiveness for scaling complex task generation and enhancing agent training.

item.title: Researchers analyze reliability and limits of innovation-residual auditing for autonomous data analysis agents, focusing on error localization, false flag control, and identifiability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This paper examines the reliability of innovation-residual auditing methods used to identify errors in autonomous data analysis agents that perform tasks like cohort selection and model fitting with minimal supervision. The study evaluates how different scoring approaches affect the ability to localize errors, the spread of error flags across operations, and procedures to control false positives without requiring a correct model fit. It also establishes fundamental limits on error detectability, showing that small errors may be indistinguishable from normal variation among sound analyses, with representation size posing a greater constraint than training data volume. The authors quantify how error detection varies depending on whether scores compare operations to immediate predecessors or longer reconstructions, and provide guidelines for choosing comparison lengths when errors accumulate gradually. They also analyze how audit guarantees weaken when models are imperfect or when analyses are selected for review based on their content. The findings highlight challenges in attributing minor errors and suggest that increasing the amount of sound training data yields diminishing improvements in detection limits due to representation dimensionality constraints.

item.title: Researchers introduce CAP framework to measure and detect preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy in 17 large language models across 12 advice domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Contrastive Anchor Probing (CAP), a framework to collect labeled data and detect preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS) in large language models (LLMs), where models reverse initial stances to align with user preferences. They applied CAP to 17 open- and closed-source LLMs, gathering 290,460 labeled responses across 12 everyday advice domains, revealing PSRS rates ranging from 5% to 56%, with more capable models showing less sycophancy. The study demonstrates that PSRS can be detected from response text alone, though detection performance declines on unseen models, highlighting challenges in cross-model generalization. The researchers propose initial solutions to this issue and plan to release their dataset and code to support further research in identifying harmful sycophantic behavior in AI systems.

item.title: Researchers propose verifier-free test-time self-correction method for LLM reasoning that refines multiple reasoning rollouts through iterative critique and majority voting, improving accuracy on math benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce a breadth-depth refinement framework for large language model (LLM) reasoning that uses test-time compute to explore and improve candidate solutions without relying on external verifiers. The method samples multiple independent reasoning rollouts, iteratively self-critiques and self-corrects each, and aggregates refined answers by majority voting, balancing diversity and error correction. Evaluated on benchmarks including AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, and MATH500, the approach consistently outperforms greedy decoding, majority voting, verifier-based selection, beam search, and lookahead decoding across several open-weight models, with notable accuracy gains such as increasing Qwen2.5-1.5B's MATH500 accuracy from 58.0% to 32.5% on AMC. These results suggest that refining sampled trajectories at test time can be more effective than simply increasing sample size or relying on verifier models.

item.title: Researchers propose INTraJ, a two-stage trajectory prediction framework separating planning and reaction, achieving state-of-the-art results on four benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce INTraJ, a unified framework for trajectory prediction that explicitly decomposes social influence into a planning stage, which anticipates others' future behaviors to construct reference trajectories, and a reaction stage, which adjusts locally based on residuals. This approach supports both multi-target and single-target prediction paradigms and demonstrates improved performance, particularly in final displacement error and long-horizon consistency, across four standard benchmarks including Argoverse 2 and ETH/UCY. The study highlights that social interactions in trajectory prediction function in staged roles, with planning preceding reaction, and validates that this decomposition leads to more stable and accurate predictions. The INTraJ code has been made publicly available for further research and application.

item.title: Researchers propose DreamGuard, a proactive runtime guardrail for LLM agents using a risk-aware world model to predict and mitigate long-horizon risks before action execution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: DreamGuard is a new runtime guardrail designed for large language model (LLM) agents that interact with external tools and real-world systems, aiming to prevent unsafe actions that could cause irreversible harm. Unlike existing reactive guardrails that assess only immediate action safety, DreamGuard uses a risk-aware world model to maintain a latent state over the agent's trajectory and predict future risks, enabling proactive intervention decisions before actions are executed. The system was evaluated across four benchmarks and an online guardrail test, outperforming reactive and other proactive baselines by achieving the best balance between safety and utility. DreamGuard also maintains low latency, averaging 25 milliseconds per call, making it efficient for real-time applications involving LLM agents.

item.title: Researchers introduce Unified Agent, a stateful AI system managing interactions across devices and time with improved state design and performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose Unified Agent, an AI system designed to manage user interactions across multiple devices and moments by maintaining a compact, action-ready state that organizes engagement evidence and requests. This approach addresses limitations in existing single-agent and multi-agent systems that struggle with scattered observations and state management across devices and time. The team developed a benchmark to compare state designs and found that Unified Agent significantly outperforms adaptations of four published designs. The system's advantage remains robust across different multimodal large language model families, capabilities, and reasoning efforts. The researchers plan to make their code and data publicly available on GitHub.

item.title: Researchers identify irreversible skill contamination in self-evolving LLM agents and propose Verifier-as-Gatekeeper to pre-commit filter harmful skills, improving performance and transferability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers found that self-evolving large language model (LLM) agents accumulate skills from their execution trajectories, but beyond a critical pool size, adding new skills can degrade performance due to irreversible contamination chains formed by defective skills. They propose Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG), a system that filters skills before admission using three critics-structural validity, behavioral harmlessness, and semantic consistency-combined with subset selection to prevent combinatorial contamination. On the Terminal-Bench 2 benchmark, VaG improved performance consistently, achieving 72% pass@1 with a skill pool five times smaller than unfiltered accumulation, and its skill pool transferred effectively to other models and benchmarks without re-evolution. Ablation studies confirmed that each critic intercepts distinct harmful skills, highlighting the necessity of pre-commit gating to maintain and improve LLM agent capabilities.

item.title: G-STEER refines personalized deep research queries using graph-scaffolded evidence grounding to improve target coverage and reduce user questions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: G-STEER is a system that refines user research requests into personalized specifications by considering user goals, constraints, and preferences before passing them to a deep research agent. It uses an Intent Elicitation Graph to model dependencies among framing factors and learns a clarification policy that balances coverage of relevant factors with the cost of acquiring evidence. Experiments demonstrate that G-STEER achieves higher weighted target coverage and better report personalization while asking about one third as many user questions compared to a strong baseline.

item.title: AppDeltaWorld introduces a transition-grounded delta code world model for mobile GUI agents, improving GUI prediction and training efficiency with state-of-the-art results on AndroidLens and other benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: AppDeltaWorld is a new world model designed for mobile GUI agents that predicts the next graphical user interface as a reachable code update rather than an unconstrained image or text. This approach addresses challenges in obtaining real interaction trajectories for sensitive apps and the limitations of existing simulated environments, such as unstable generation and inconsistent action-transition logic. The model retrieves app-specific HTML references and generates executable HTML conditioned on current screen data and predicted next-screen text, enhancing fidelity and UI element reconstruction compared to previous methods. The model achieves the highest fidelity on the CMGUIBench-500 benchmark under Code2World evaluation and supports filtered closed-loop supervised fine-tuning data construction. Combined with public supervision, this enables the AppDeltaAgent to reach state-of-the-art performance on AndroidLens and consistent improvements on MobileGym and MobileWorld. Additionally, test-time reinforcement learning based on the world model allows policy adaptation and further performance gains without requiring additional real app interactions.

item.title: Researchers investigate Vision Language Models for annotating video game frames with reward signals, finding challenges in accuracy and exploring optimization techniques [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied the use of Vision Language Models (VLMs) to annotate video game frame sequences with reward signals, aiming to support applications like conditioned training and offline reinforcement learning. They found that VLMs often struggle to answer basic questions in racing games and other genres, limiting their effectiveness in synthetic gaming environments. The study examined factors affecting annotation quality, including input sequence length, resolution, and question batching, and proposed countermeasures such as VLM output mixing and prompt optimization to improve performance. These findings highlight challenges in applying VLMs to video game data annotation due to variability in synthetic scenarios and differences from real-world physics.

item.title: Researchers train a conditioned video game agent using offline reinforcement learning on a dataset annotated by Vision Language Models extracting human-defined rewards [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose using Vision Language Models (VLMs) to annotate video game datasets with human-defined rewards to address challenges in reinforcement learning (RL), such as the need for game engine access and sparse rewards. They demonstrate that offline RL can train an agent conditioned to respond to these annotated rewards. The study discusses early experimental difficulties and limitations encountered in this approach, highlighting potential avenues for simplifying policy learning in video games.

item.title: Researchers propose a Temporal-Enhanced framework with bidirectional alignment to improve climate data super-resolution by capturing temporal correlations and reducing noise [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a new Temporal-Enhanced framework that uses bidirectional temporal alignment to improve the spatial resolution of climate data super-resolution (SR). This approach addresses limitations in existing deep learning methods that focus mainly on single-frame spatial information and often overlook temporal correlations, which are crucial for enhancing SR outcomes in noisy and stochastic climate data. The framework includes Paired Latent Mapping for spatial alignment and noise reduction by unifying latent spaces, and Bidirectional Temporal Alignment that captures temporal correlations through forward and backward network training on consecutive latent frames. Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets demonstrated that this method outperforms previous approaches in generating fine-grained climate data from low-resolution inputs, which is vital for meteorological predictions and decision support across various domains.

item.title: Researchers propose AgentOPSD, a recursive self-distillation method for turn-level credit assignment in agentic reinforcement learning, outperforming baselines on ALFWorld and other benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: AgentOPSD is a critic-free, recursive approach that aggregates token-level teacher-student log-probability gaps into turn-level evidence and updates a Bayesian belief state to assign credit in multi-turn reinforcement learning tasks. It converts sparse outcome supervision into detailed turn-level credit signals without requiring additional critics or rollouts. Evaluations on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA using Qwen2.5 models at 3B and 7B scales show AgentOPSD surpasses GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines, achieving 89.1% success on ALFWorld with the 7B model. Ablation studies attribute performance gains to turn-level aggregation and history-dependent recursive belief updates.

item.title: Researchers propose a six-level implementation roadmap for Economic World Models to simulate economies with adaptive agents and evolving institutions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This paper presents a systems blueprint for Economic World Models (EWMs), which simulate economic dynamics by modeling heterogeneous agents, their interactions, and institutional mechanisms. The authors organize EWMs into a six-level capability ladder ranging from fixed rule-based agents to adaptive, self-evolving agents and sim-to-real economic twins aligned with real-world data. A literature survey shows most existing work focuses on lower-level simulations, with advanced features like self-evolving agents and validated economic mechanisms still rare. The paper aims to accelerate development of high-fidelity economic simulation environments for decision-making and AI training, releasing curated resources to support future research.

item.title: Researchers integrate implicit and explicit relational biases using graph-based multiple instance learning to improve skin lesion diagnosis accuracy on ISIC-2018 and ISIC-2019 datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This study presents a dual-level relational framework combining implicit representation learning with explicit structural modeling to enhance image classification for skin lesion diagnosis. Using an EfficientNetB3 baseline, the researchers applied a patch-based convolutional masked autoencoder to learn implicit inter-patch relationships and incorporated explicit graph-based message passing with various graph topologies. Experiments on ISIC-2018 and ISIC-2019 benchmarks showed that integrating implicit and explicit relational modeling improved balanced accuracy from 76.17% to 79.27% on ISIC-2018 and from 59.84% to 60.67% on ISIC-2019. The approach demonstrates that combining implicit and explicit relational biases through graph-based learning can enhance diagnostic performance in medical imaging tasks.

item.title: Researchers present ECHO, a locally deployable conversational health assistant with temporal memory, safety guardrails, and speech assessment for chronic care management [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: ECHO (Enhanced Care & Health Observer) is a conversational health assistant designed for long-term chronic care that runs locally on consumer hardware without transmitting patient data externally, supporting GDPR and KVKK compliance. It integrates an agentic chatbot with 17 clinical tools and a temporal knowledge graph for persistent memory, achieving a 94.9% tool-execution pass rate on a 59-scenario benchmark using GPT-5 Mini. The system includes a two-stage hybrid safety layer combining a rule-based filter for crisis signals and jailbreak attempts with a signed graph neural network that classifies clinical intent, reaching 88.8% accuracy and 90.6% unsafe recall on a Turkish health dataset. Additionally, a multimodal speech assessment module uses Whisper acoustic encoding and BERT text encoding with cross-attention fusion to estimate emotion, depression, and pain, achieving a mean macro F1 score of 0.652.

item.title: Researchers introduce Poli-Bias, a framework measuring political bias in large language models by comparing responses to legally equivalent international conflict scenarios with swapped country identities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Poli-Bias, a counterfactual framework designed to measure political bias in large language models (LLMs) by evaluating whether these models treat legally equivalent international conflict scenarios differently based on the countries involved. The framework compares paired prompts with systematically swapped country identities across various geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and reasoning tasks, decomposing response disparities into five interpretable dimensions to reveal unequal treatment. Testing 13 contemporary LLMs from diverse families and sizes, the study found that country identities and user affiliations can systematically influence how equivalent actions are described, evaluated, and defended under international law. Poli-Bias offers a fine-grained method for auditing political even-handedness and sycophancy in LLMs, addressing challenges in capturing subtle biases through a single metric.

item.title: Researchers present schema-based framework using generative AI for hierarchical information extraction and semantic evaluation, achieving over 90% F1 score on health assessment documents with significant speedup [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers developed a schema-guided framework that uses generative AI to extract complex, structured information from unstructured text in a single zero-shot model call, followed by automated semantic evaluation against a gold standard. The approach encodes domain knowledge in a schema to systematically extract hierarchical, nested attributes with variable cardinality and uses a path-based semantic matching algorithm for evaluation. Using the Claude Opus 3 model, the framework extracted 12 of 14 attributes from NICE health technology assessment documents with an F1 score above 90%, completing the task about 30 times faster than human experts. The study also demonstrates the framework's generalizability across different AI models, organizations, and languages.

item.title: TS-RAG: Retrieval Augmented Generation for Time Series Forecasting [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.06223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While deep learning models, particularly transformer-based architectures, have shown impressive performance in time series forecasting, the application of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in this domain remains limited. Since RAG has proven effective in enhancing the capabilities of large language models by incorporating relevant external information, retrieving similar time series sequences as references might also improve accuracy in time series forecasting tasks. However, most time series models are constrained by limited training data, smaller parameter scales, and a lack of the extensive generative capabilities found in large language models. Simply concatenating reference sequences into the prompt, as done in language models, may not yield the expected results. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach, TS-RAG, which leverages RAG to enhance forecasting performance. The framework introduces specially designed reference tokens to effectively fuse information from the input sequence with that from retrieved similar sequences, enabling a more robust capture of complex temporal dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate that TS-RAG achieves consistent state-of-the-art performance across several real-world forecasting benchmarks.

item.title: Improving the Realism of Synthetic Clinical Benchmarks Under Utility Constraints [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.06265v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Synthetic clinical benchmarks for enterprise AI agents can pass existing utility checks and still remain structurally unrealistic, especially in privacy-sensitive healthcare settings where operational data are hard to access. We study how to improve such benchmarks without breaking the downstream utility checks already used in practice. We formulate benchmark revision as utility-constrained realism improvement: dataset changes should increase realism while staying above an operational utility floor. We instantiate this idea on a care-gap benchmark derived from Synthea-generated patients exercised through demonstration electronic health record workflows and then processed by the same downstream pipeline as operational data. Realism is measured through missingness structure, simplicity, structural plausibility, and population alignment. The baseline benchmark is extremely thin: sampled-pair missingness is 79.44%, only 12.75% of rows are actionable, 38.94% of patients have zero actionable measures, and top-three token concentration reaches 100.0%. Two deterministic revisions improve these panels while remaining above the current utility floor, whereas a naive densification control preserves unrealistic templating. We further show that internal benchmark realism and source fidelity to an aggregate operational reference are related but distinct objectives. These results suggest that synthetic benchmark quality should be optimized explicitly, with utility treated as one constraint rather than as sufficient evidence of realism.

item.title: Beyond Top-K: Replacing Black-Box Retrieval with Interpretable Agentic Operations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.06305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation over long documents is dominated by one design: chunk the text, embed the chunks, and surface the top-k nearest neighbours of the query. We argue that for an important class of documents -- financial statements, audit reports, regulatory returns -- this design is structurally unsound, and we make the argument measurable. On a 780-page government financial report, 86.8% of content lines are table rows, thousands of near-identical figures compete in one embedding space, and a figure inherits its unit from a header a median of 13 lines above it -- so a chunk boundary routinely separates a number from whether it is in lakh or crore, an error of two orders of magnitude. A table-aware chunker built as a steelman fixes the unit problem but leaves 27-30% of numeric chunks with no fiscal-year header at every chunk size we tried. We propose READ (Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search), in which an agent reads the raw document through three deterministic operations -- normalized lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded span reads -- exposed over the Model Context Protocol, so a trajectory is a replayable audit trail, not an opaque similarity score. On 51 verified questions READ answers 58.8% against dense retrieval's 15.7% (p_Holm = 2 x 10^-5) -- or 35.3% tuned, which READ still leads by 23.5 points (p_Holm = 0.017). An agent given the same loop but a top-k tool reaches only 27.5%, locating the gain in the interface rather than in iteration. We also report what the evidence does not support: BM25 is statistically indistinguishable from READ, so our result separates embedding-based from embedding-free retrieval, not agentic from lexical search.

item.title: Tracing the Heart: An Evidence-Linked Pipeline for Heart-Failure Feature Engineering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.06366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electronic health record (EHR) feature engineering is a major bottleneck in clinical research and AI, accounting for 39-45% of data scientists' workload. This is especially pronounced in heart failure, which affects an estimated 6.7 million U.S. adults and requires integrating fragmented EHR data with disease-specific, guideline-based clinical reasoning. Existing rule-based and large language model (LLM)-based approaches offer only partial automation with limited maintainability and evidence traceability. We developed the Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), an evidence-linked, rubric-grounded pipeline for automated heart-failure feature engineering, and evaluated it on 500 dummy patient records from nine EHR source tables. nMAS generated 132 structured and 70 rubric-scored aggregated features, verified for structural integrity, rubric compliance, and provenance, and audited by a restricted LLM. Adding the aggregated features improved held-out AUROC from 0.895 to 0.963 for HFrEF and 0.870 to 0.910 for HFpEF phenotyping, and an independent LLM-based rubric assessment of evidence support and methodological soundness scored the features at 81.5% of maximum points. These results demonstrate the feasibility of automated, auditable feature engineering for complex cardiovascular EHR data, though evaluation was limited to a single-institution cohort and external validation is needed.

item.title: Simulator-Grounded Large Language Models for Industrial Causal Reasoning: Tool-Use, Structured Injection, and Plant-Portable Retrieval for Wastewater Treatment Decision Support [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wastewater operators need answers grounded in how their plant's variables interact and how fast effects propagate, not in generic pretraining text, when asking causal questions such as "why is N2O rising?" or "what happens if I cut aeration by 20%?". We compare three concrete ways to ground a frozen Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct model in an architecturally interpretable wastewater simulator (CCSS-IX): a live simulator oracle (Method 1), structured parameter injection (Method 2), and a Decoupled Recall-Reasoning (DRR) retriever (Method 3). On a 198-question causal benchmark the three reach 99.5%, 79%, and 75.8%, forming a deployment ladder above the strongest retrieval-augmented baseline at 48%. The DRR retriever has 110M parameters and trains per plant in ~17 seconds; after cross-plant transfer to a biologically distinct plant it still reaches 88%, while Method 2's static table cannot transfer. On a 60-question counterfactual benchmark only Method 3 handles queries about what happens after an intervention: +16.3 pp over Method 2, paired 95% CI [+7.1, +26.4] pp, with 100% on the timescale and operating-regime categories. On the AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC) with an OpenBookQA fact corpus, the same selective-retrieval mechanism reaches 79% versus unconstrained Llama-3.1-8B 76% and full-injection 74%, a +3 pp out-of-domain replication that argues against a result specific to wastewater treatment. We provide the first single-simulator comparison of live tool-use, static parameter injection, and learned numerical-parameter retrieval for industrial causal question answering.

item.title: Mean-Field Dynamics of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with chain-of-thought reasoning have been widely applied in recent years, and theoretical explanations of their behavior may help deepen our understanding and guide model optimization. In this study, we introduce a framework that seeks statistical regularities and theoretical interpretations in LLM reasoning without simplifying the model architecture or making analogies to existing physical systems. We formulate LLM reasoning as a guided discovery process on a clue graph, and derive a one-dimensional ordinary differential equation for the fraction of discovered clues using the mean-field approximation. Experimentally, clue tokens are identified using the normalized surprisal of a student LLM on the outputs of a teacher LLM, and statistical regularities are obtained by averaging over many reasoning chains of thought. Our experiments show that the resulting statistical regularities are reproducible within the same dataset and can be fitted by the solving the proposed theoretical equation.

item.title: Universal Pathologies, Conditional Consequences: A Triple-Robustness Analysis of RAG for Multi-Hop Traceability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GraphRAG underperforms vector RAG on citation precision in many reports, but where and why have remained corpus-bound. We present a triple-robustness analysis that holds the retrieval architecture fixed and varies three orthogonal axes embedder (local e5-small -> Azure text-embedding-3-small), corpus (DO-178C typed-edge requirements -> Wikipedia paragraph chains via MuSiQue), and judge (paired GPT-5.4 x GPT-4.1) across 4,440 main-matrix runs, 600 cross-corpus runs, and 1,200 paired faithfulness judgments. (C2a) Over-citation is architecturally universal: GraphRAG emits 11-15 IDs per answer at citation precision 0.12-0.23 and retrieval recall 0.68-0.87 across all three settings. (C2b) Its faithfulness consequence is corpus-conditional: in typed-edge DO-178C, GraphRAG faithfulness collapses 74%->40% across hops; on Wikipedia chains the same pipeline rises 42%->58% because over-cited paragraphs remain topically supporting. (C1) Stratum-conditional winners are corpus-conditional but embedder-robust: vanilla wins 2-hop on DO-178C, GraphRAG wins 2-hop on MuSiQue, identical under either embedder. (C3) Single-judge LLM faithfulness is fragile to retrieval state: same-judge self-kappa across embedders is 0.137 for GPT-5.4 (verdict change on 41% of items). A learned router on dense embeddings alone reaches macro-F1 0.86 on hop classification (C4). We argue triple-robustness is the minimum bar for trustworthy RAG architecture claims.

item.title: Beyond Sentiment: Comparing Traditional NLP and LLM-Based Multi-Dimensional Analysis for Political News Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional sentiment analysis (SA) models, while effective for polarity classification, provide limited insight into the rhetorical, ideological, and framing dimensions of political discourse -- dimensions that are central to research in the social sciences and humanities (SSH). In this paper, we present a comparative study of RoBERTa-based sentiment analysis and an LLM-based multi-dimensional framing analysis platform applied to a corpus of 50 political news articles from 17 international media outlets. The results reveal a critical limitation we term neutral collapse: RoBERTa classifies 70% of articles as neutral, effectively flattening substantively rich political content into an analytically uninformative category. We find that 23% of neutral-classified articles exhibit negative probability scores above 0.30. By contrast, the LLM-based approach captures political bias direction and intensity, sensationalism, emotional appeal, and political framing -- yielding multi-dimensional analytical outputs aligned with SSH epistemologies. We argue that for political media analysis, traditional SA alone is insufficient, and that LLM-based multi-dimensional frameworks offer a more epistemologically adequate computational lens for SSH research needs.

item.title: Large Language Models Threaten Double-blind Review [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05157v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Double blind peer review serves as the scientific community primary defense against status and affiliation bias. Its effectiveness rests on the assumption that anonymized manuscripts convey scientific merit without revealing their authors. While authorship can often be recovered using citation networks or stylistic markers, we show that this assumption is increasingly fragile in the presence of large language models (LLMs). Using only titles and abstracts from papers published after model training, we find that LLMs collapse anonymity more efficiently than humans, with belief concentrating onto a small subset of plausible authors drawn from pools of five domain expert candidates. This vulnerability persists even when stylistic and bibliographic cues are excluded, indicating that stable patterns in problem framing and research focus function as latent conceptual signatures of authorship. Together, these findings indicate that double blind review is vulnerable to automated semantic inference, necessitating a revaluation of how anonymity and fairness are maintained in an AI augmented research ecosystem.

item.title: DREAM: LLM-based Dynamic Role-playing via Event-Aware Memory Graph [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Role-playing agents (RPAs) have emerged as a key application of large language models, enabling immersive and high-fidelity character simulation. Accurate role-playing of established characters requires not only stylistic imitation but also temporally consistent and causally grounded behavioral reasoning. However, existing RPAs primarily rely on static character descriptions and unstructured memory, limiting their ability to maintain long-term narrative and personality coherence. We introduce DREAM, a structured memory framework for role-playing agents inspired by the Activating Event-Belief-Consequence (ABC) cognitive model. DREAM transforms unstructured literary text into an Event-aware Memory Graph (EMG) that organizes character experiences into temporally ordered and causally linked event graph. This representation enables the construction of dynamic, dual-granularity character profiles that capture both stable personality traits and event-driven behavioral evolution. We further propose the Temporal Causal Memory (TCM) benchmark to evaluate temporal consistency and long-range causal narrative coherence. DREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance across CoSER, LIFECHOICE, and TCM, outperforming multiple strong baselines. Our approach demonstrates the effectiveness of structured memory in enhancing the interpretability and consistency of role-playing agents.

item.title: Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05176v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Music education has never been a static discipline. Each major technological shift has forced educators and institutions to reconsider what they teach, how they teach it, and why. We now stand at what may be the most consequential of such turning points. Three deeply intertwined transformations have been converging simultaneously: 1. The very nature of music has changed: how it is made, distributed, consumed, and valued; 2. The public for music has changed: listening habits are now shaped by streaming algorithms and the boundary between consumer and creator has blurred; 3. Music-making itself has changed: digital audio workstations (DAWs) have for two decades been reshaping compositional practice. In addition, generative AI has now irrupted, capable of producing complete, stylistically coherent musical pieces from a short text prompt. These changes are not independent of one another, and they all bear directly on musical education - both the content that must be taught, and the pedagogical tools and methods available to teach it. This paper attempts to map these challenges and to consider how education might adapt. Section 2 surveys the changes in various aspects of music (nature, production, public, economics). Section 3 examines the implications for education before Section 4 concludes.

item.title: Position: It's Time to Optimize LLMs for Self-Consistency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite ever-increasing sophistication in language model (LM) pre- and post-training pipelines, many important failures persist: models overcondition on user framing ("sycophancy"), exhibit incomplete logical generalization, and produce confident but incorrect responses. We argue that these failures arise from a modeling assumption permeating all aspects of the pipeline: that behavior can be specified and evaluated independently on single-output pairs. Many model failures are difficult, if not impossible, to detect without reasoning about relationships between a model's responses across inputs. In this position paper, we propose self-consistency as a framework for understanding these failures. We first observe that a wide variety of techniques designed to improve specific aspects of LM behavior-targeting properties as diverse as adversarial robustness and factual coherence-can be understood as special cases of a common "consistency optimization" procedure and addressed with a standard set of optimization tools. We next outline a set of new model properties that could be achieved by optimizing for consistency, and conclude with a discussion of what it would mean to develop generally consistent LMs, including the capabilities they would enable and the objections they raise.

item.title: Quality Diversity for Reliable Data Driven Time-Use Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05230v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The daily allocation of the finite 24-hour time budget is strongly associated with physical, mental, and cognitive health. While predictive models can estimate the relationship between time-use compositions and health outcomes such as body mass index, life satisfaction, and cognition, most optimization approaches focus only on maximizing expected benefit and do not consider the uncertainty inherent in data-driven prediction. Ignoring uncertainty in health-related decisions can lead to unrealistic time-use recommendations. To address this gap, we introduce an uncertainty quantification Quality Diversity (QD) framework for a more reliable time-use recommendation. Objective functions are derived using compositional data analysis using a large child cohort dataset n > 1000, to capture the relationship between daily activity compositions and multiple health indicators. We develop a new approach that incorporates predictive uncertainty into QD processes and produces more reliable recommendations that balance the expected health benefits with the confidence of the model. We explore the solution space through variable-based and objective-based behavioral representations, revealing diverse high-quality time-use composition and explicit relationships between health outcomes under uncertainty. By embedding uncertainty directly into optimization, our framework shifts the time-use recommendations toward regions of lower uncertainty while preserving high-quality structures for more reliable decision-making in behavioral health.

item.title: One Qubit Can Beat One Bit: Quantum Advantage for Post-Training Quantization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05240v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: One-bit post-training quantization represents each weight using only its sign, requiring all deployment contexts to share the same binary weight matrix even when their activation statistics favor different sign patterns. We study this shared-sign constraint and introduce Quantum Random Access Quantization (QRAQ). This framework encodes context-dependent signs in a quantum random-access code and retrieves them via context-matched Pauli measurements. Under an explicit fresh-copy logical readout model, QRAQ produces an unbiased, context-specific binary surrogate with a tractable shot-noise penalty. We prove a row-wise separation from shared-sign one-bit PTQ with signed per-row scales. When the optimal context-wise signs are incompatible, QRAQ achieves a strictly lower ideal reconstruction risk. We also derive finite-shot and calibrated-noise conditions under which this separation is retained. Fixed-readout quantum schemes are classically simulable, so the relevant resource in this model is measurement incompatibility rather than quantization alone. Finally, we characterize the role of scale granularity, provide finite-sample certificates, and evaluate the predicted ideal, finite-shot, noisy, and multi-context regimes in simulator experiments.

item.title: Marginal Matching Does Not License Factorized Sampling: Auditing Conditional Style Leakage in Factorized Generative Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05243v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Factorized generative models commonly regularize a latent style variable z_s by matching its marginal distribution to a fixed Gaussian prior and interpret this as evidence that the style representation is independent of class information. We show that this interpretation is incorrect. Matching only the marginal distribution places no constraint on the class-conditional distributions, allowing the latent style to remain highly predictive of the label despite appearing perfectly Gaussian in aggregate. We derive an exact decomposition showing that this mismatch is one of four conditions required for factorized sampling, and demonstrate that eliminating it is necessary but not sufficient to obtain the intended factorization. Empirically, our case-study model and four representative latent baselines achieve near-zero global MMD while still allowing a linear probe to recover class labels with 74%--100% accuracy (10% chance level). Our model reaches 99.15% clustering accuracy, whereas externally evaluated class-conditional generation succeeds only 16% of the time. This leakage remains under six independent perturbations involving model capacity, curriculum, prior geometry, and supervision across two datasets. Four mitigation strategies reduce probe accuracy to 21%--46%, although they leave within-class dependence largely unchanged. A post-hoc conditional prior improves externally evaluated class generation to 0.97 on MNIST without retraining but reaches only 0.41 on CIFAR-10, while an empirical style bank achieves 0.88 on CIFAR-10. These results demonstrate that no divergence computed solely on the marginal distribution of the style latent can certify independence from class labels, and that reporting marginal statistics alone does not verify the property commonly claimed in factorized generative models.

item.title: PRISM: Priority-aware Rubric Internalization via Structured Multimodal Data Synthesis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05249v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-world multimodal instructions often bundle multiple requirements with unequal importance, yet most multimodal training data still reduce instruction following to answering one self-contained question. We study this gap through \textbf{rubric comprehension}, which casts the model not as a generator measured against rubrics but as an \textbf{executor} that follows them: given an image and a typed, prioritized rubric, the model must verify each rule before producing an overall judgment. To support this setting, we propose \textbf{PRISM}, a four-stage data synthesis framework that produces persona--task pairs, prefix-guided rule sets, quality-filtered rubrics, and structured verification traces. We further introduce \textbf{PRISM-Eval}, whose Loose and Strict metrics use deterministic matching against fixed labels and therefore require no inference-time judge model. With only 10K synthesized samples, PRISM lifts Qwen3-VL-4B from 9.5\% to 30.1\% Strict accuracy on PRISM-Eval while preserving average performance on general benchmarks, and the gains transfer to four additional open-source MLLMs across dense and MoE architectures, suggesting that structured rubric supervision is a scalable path toward multi-rule, priority-aware multimodal instruction following.

item.title: An Emerging Retail Portfolio Management Application: Personalized, Tax-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Natural Language Goals [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retail investors lack access to the kind of personalized, tax-aware portfolio management that institutional clients take for granted -- existing robo-advisors use static, rule-based allocation, and institutional-grade systems require account minimums and technology stacks unavailable to individual investors. We present a fully built, integration-tested application that closes this gap: a FastAPI backend and web dashboard that let a user describe an investment goal in plain language (e.g. "I want steady growth but need to sell some shares next month for a down payment"), routes that goal to one of six investment mandates, and produces a live, broker-integrated portfolio recommendation from athree-phase reinforcement learning system -- a self-supervised cross-asset encoder, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) allocation policy with a learned intent router, and a lightweight LoRA adapter that personalizes recommendations from an individual's revealed brokerage behavior without retraining the shared model. The system is functionally complete and integration-tested end-to-end against a live brokerage API (Alpaca, paper-trading mode), including multi-user authentication, a trust first preview-before-apply confirmation flow, daily email digests, and an auditable action-integrity chain, but has not yet been opened to real end-users; we report this honestly as an emerging, pre-deployment application with a concrete path to full deployment, alongside 14-day walk-forward backtests (bootstrapped confidence intervals included) as preliminary, pre-deployment validation rather than production performance. We also report several practical engineering lessons -- silently-inactive integration paths, hanging third-party API calls, and the value of end-to-end empirical verification over trusting checkpoint metadata -- that we believe generalize to other applied RL systems built on external, live data sources.

item.title: Failing Gracefully: Mitigating Impact of Inevitable Robot Failures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05313v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Service robots operate in household environments shared with humans, pets, and everyday objects, where they are highly susceptible to failures such as software crashes, hardware degradation, or unpredictable interactions.
